lessons.title: Start at Main

blocks.label: The starting point
blocks.simple: The program begins inside Main. The first job is to create the sample projects. At line 16, C# runs the instructions on the right of the equals sign first. CreateSampleProjects must finish before projects can receive its result.
blocks.technical: Main is the entry point. It is static, so the runtime can call it without creating a Program object. CreateSampleProjects is another static method in Program; the class name is omitted because we are already inside that class. Its return type is List<Project>. The local variable projects receives a reference to that list, whose elements refer to Project objects.
blocks.why: Keeping sample construction in a named method makes Main read as a sequence of jobs. We could put every sample value directly in Main, but that would bury the menu underneath setup data. A List is convenient for looping and selection; an array of three Projects would also work for this fixed demo.
blocks.before: Main has started. The local projects variable has not yet received a value.
blocks.after: After the call finishes: projects refers to one list containing the Website, Inventory, and Training Project references.
blocks.say: Execution starts in Main. I call CreateSampleProjects to build the sample data, then store the returned list in projects. List<Project> is a type, projects is a variable, and CreateSampleProjects() is a method call.
rows: public static async Task Main()
This declares the starting method; it is not creating a project task.
public controls access; static removes the need for a Program instance; async allows await inside the method; Task represents completion without a result value. Main takes no arguments here.
List<Project>
A list whose entries point to Project objects.
List<T> is a generic .NET class. Substituting Project for T restricts its elements to Project references; this is not a method call.
projects = CreateSampleProjects();
Ask the sample-data method for a list, then name that list reference projects.
The call expression on the right is evaluated before assignment. Parentheses invoke the method; the empty argument list supplies no inputs; the semicolon terminates the statement.

lessons.title: Create the project objects

blocks.label: Call the Project constructor
blocks.simple: Website already exists. At this line, new Project starts creating the Inventory object by calling its constructor with three identity values. Follow the next block into that constructor before reading the initializer below this line.
blocks.technical: new Project(2, "Inventory System", "Taylor Smith") invokes Project(int id, string name, string manager). This is an instance-creation expression. The constructor’s parameters receive these argument values. Its object initializer and the later status-change calls have not executed yet.
blocks.why: One Project object keeps one project’s facts together. Using separate unrelated variables for every project would make it harder to pass the right facts to methods. The deliberate fixed one-task/one-milestone/one-risk design avoids a second collection of item objects, at the cost of not supporting multiple risks.
blocks.before: The constructor arguments are 2, Inventory System, and Taylor Smith. Inventory has not been fully initialized.
blocks.after: Control enters Project’s constructor. The caller is waiting at Program.cs line 332; the remaining properties will be assigned afterward.
blocks.say: This new expression starts one Project object. I pass ID, name and manager into the constructor, which runs before the initializer and status changes.
rows: Project inventory = new Project(...)
Make one Project object and keep a way to reach it in inventory.
The left Project is the variable’s type. new invokes a constructor. The string arguments are literals. Passing these values does not change the class definition; it initializes one instance.

blocks.label: The constructor called by new Project(...)
blocks.simple: A constructor is the setup code that runs when new Project(...) creates an object. The values from the call arrive in the lowercase input names id, name, and manager. The assignments copy them into this object’s uppercase properties.
blocks.technical: Project(int id, string name, string manager) is a constructor: it has the class name and no return type. Parameters belong to this invocation; Id, Name, and Manager are instance properties that remain on the object after the constructor finishes. C# is case-sensitive, so Id and id are distinct identifiers. Id = id is equivalent here to this.Id = id.
blocks.why: The constructor requires identity values at creation time, instead of depending on a later setup method. Other demonstration values are assigned with an initializer. This is simple initialization, not comprehensive validation: empty names or duplicate IDs are not rejected by this constructor.
blocks.before: The call passes id = 2, name = Inventory System, manager = Taylor Smith.
blocks.after: This object has Id 2, Name Inventory System, Manager Taylor Smith. Execution returns to the object initializer in Program.
blocks.say: The constructor gives every new Project its starting identity. Lowercase names are the values coming in, and uppercase names are the properties on the object that keep those values.
rows: public Project(int id, string name, string manager)
Three named inputs are required when creating a Project.
The constructor is public so Program can call it. A parameter is the input name in this definition; an argument is the concrete value supplied at the call site.
Id = id;
Save the incoming number on this object.
Assignment reads the right-hand parameter and invokes the property setter on the current instance. It is not an equality comparison.
Name = name;
Save this project’s own name.
The Name property retains the string value after the local constructor parameter goes out of scope. Another Project instance can hold a different Name.
Manager = manager;
Save this project’s manager, then finish setup.
Reaching the constructor’s closing brace returns control to object creation; a constructor does not declare a separate return value.

blocks.label: Resume in Program: assign properties, then set statuses
blocks.simple: The constructor has finished. The object initializer now fills Inventory’s task, milestone and risk properties. Then ChangeStatus sets the task to InProgress and opens the risk. Each assignment affects this one object.
blocks.technical: The initializer runs after the Project constructor returns. Each property name on the left targets the newly created instance. After the initializer completes, inventory receives its reference, and the following instance-method calls apply validated status changes. Those calls are not part of the constructor.
blocks.why: One Project object keeps one project’s facts together. Using separate unrelated variables for every project would make it harder to pass the right facts to methods. The deliberate fixed one-task/one-milestone/one-risk design avoids a second collection of item objects, at the cost of not supporting multiple risks.
blocks.before: The new object has ID 2, its name and manager. Work statuses default to NotStarted and risk defaults to Closed.
blocks.after: Inventory’s task is InProgress; its risk is Open; likelihood is 4 and impact is 5. CreateSampleProjects next creates Training, then returns the list.
blocks.say: new Project creates one object from the Project class. The constructor sets its ID, name and manager; the initializer fills the remaining properties. The task and risk are properties on this object, not separate custom objects.
rows: TaskTitle / TaskOwner / TaskDueDate (separate assignments)
These are three different facts about this project’s one task.
They are properties assigned by the object initializer after construction. AddDays(7) returns a new DateTime seven days after today; it does not change DateTime.Today.
RiskLikelihood and RiskImpact initializers
The classroom example supplies two ratings in advance.
These are ordinary integer assignments, not predictions from Qwen. Their product is 20. These public setters do not validate every assignment.
inventory.ChangeStatus(1, ItemStatus.InProgress)
Set Inventory’s task status using the project’s validation method.
inventory is the receiver object. 1 and ItemStatus.InProgress are arguments. The method’s bool result is unused during this known-valid sample setup.
inventory.ChangeStatus(3, ItemStatus.Open)
Open the one risk on Inventory.
Section 3 selects RiskStatus. Every new Project starts with a Closed risk, so this explicit call makes this sample Open.

lessons.title: Return to Main with the list

blocks.label: Give the result back
blocks.simple: After making all three projects, this line creates one list with three entries and gives the list back to Main. It does not print the list. It also does not create three more Project objects.
blocks.technical: new List<Project> { website, inventory, training } uses a collection initializer. It adds the existing object references in that order. The method returns the list reference to its caller; the Project objects remain reachable through that list after the local sample-variable names leave scope.
blocks.why: Returning a list gives Main one value to pass around. If we copied all properties into new objects on every selection, edits could affect a copy rather than the object in the menu. This version deliberately shares references to the same objects.
blocks.before: website, inventory and training each refer to a constructed Project.
blocks.after: The returned list has Count = 3 and indexes 0, 1, 2. Project ID 2 is a property value, not a list index.
blocks.say: This returns one list containing the three existing Project references. Main receives the list; it does not receive three separate return values.
rows: new List<Project> { website, inventory, training }
Put the existing projects together in order.
The new object here is the List, not another Project. The elements are reference values; indexes begin at zero.
return
Give this result to the method that called us.
return terminates CreateSampleProjects. Execution resumes at the suspended call expression in Main, line 16. Returning from this helper does not exit the application.

blocks.label: Main resumes after the call
blocks.simple: We are back in Main after the sample-data method returned. The list now has a name, projects. The next line makes a different kind of object: HttpClient, the reusable sender for later local AI requests. No AI request has been sent yet.
blocks.technical: This is a resume point, not a second call to CreateSampleProjects. The HttpClient reference is stored in client. A using declaration disposes this client when Main’s scope ends. Timeout is a TimeSpan property configured to 120 seconds per request. WriteLine then prints ordinary fixed text.
blocks.why: Creating one HttpClient for the application avoids making a fresh sender for every AI menu choice. Setting a finite timeout provides a bounded wait. The same client is passed as an argument to later methods; it is not a model or an API credential.
blocks.before: CreateSampleProjects has just returned to line 16.
blocks.after: projects refers to the list, client refers to an HttpClient, and the application title has been printed.
blocks.say: Main now has the project list. It creates one HttpClient for the later AI connection, sets its timeout, and prints the heading. Constructing HttpClient alone does not contact Bionic.
rows: List<Project> projects = ...
The returned list is assigned here.
The right-hand call has completed. The local variable now contains its reference; the program continues at line 18.
using HttpClient client = new HttpClient();
Create one request-sending object and arrange to clean it up at the end.
This using is resource lifetime management. It is different from using System.Text.Json at the top of the file, which imports type names.
client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(120);
Limit how long an HTTP request can wait.
The dot selects the Timeout property on this particular client. The static FromSeconds method constructs a duration value; it does not sleep for 120 seconds.
Console.WriteLine(...)
Put a line of text in the console window.
WriteLine is a static .NET method. It displays data but returns no result value. The following \n in a string inserts a line break.

lessons.title: The menu chooses a method

blocks.label: Read the menu choice and call its method
blocks.simple: The menu keeps coming back because it is inside while (true). When you type 3 and press Enter, ReadLine gives the text "3" to choice. switch finds case "3" and calls UpdateStatus. That method runs before the menu can repeat.
blocks.technical: ReadLine returns string? because input can end and produce null. The explicit null check protects Trim. switch compares the cleaned string with menu literals. A method call runs the selected action; break leaves switch and the while loop repeats. return in case five or null ends Main.
blocks.why: A switch is easy to inspect for five fixed menu commands. A dictionary of delegates would add another concept without helping this small app. Trimming accepts inputs like " 3 ". Handling null avoids repeatedly prompting after redirected input ends.
blocks.before: The title has printed. No menu choice has been read yet.
blocks.after: For input "3": UpdateStatus receives the existing list. Main is waiting for that call to finish.
blocks.say: The loop repeats the menu. ReadLine reads text, and switch picks a method based on that text. Choosing three calls UpdateStatus; choosing five returns from Main and exits.
rows: while (true)
Keep repeating this menu until a return ends Main.
true never becomes false here. Exiting relies on the explicit return branches rather than a changing loop condition.
string? choice = Console.ReadLine();
Wait for the user’s typed line; it might be absent.
? is a nullable-reference annotation. An empty line is "", while null means the input stream ended; they are different values.
switch (choice)
Choose the case matching the typed text.
Trim is performed on the previous line only if choice is not null. The switch then compares the resulting string with menu literals.
UpdateStatus(projects); then break;
Run the status-update method and then leave the switch.
The menu case and its method call and break are on separate lines. break leaves switch; the while loop continues.
await ReviewRiskAsync(projects, client);
Wait for the AI menu action to finish.
Main awaits the returned Task before reaching break and the next menu round.
case "5" or case null → return;
Exit for menu five or end-of-input.
return ends Main. This differs from break, which only leaves switch.

lessons.title: Select Inventory System

blocks.label: UpdateStatus pauses while SelectProject works
blocks.simple: UpdateStatus needs to know which Project you mean. It calls SelectProject and temporarily waits. If that selection returns a project, selectedProject refers to it. If selection was cancelled or invalid, the returned value is null and this update stops immediately.
blocks.technical: This is a private static void method. It is callable within Program without a Program instance and has no result value. The parameter projects receives the list reference by value. SelectProject returns Project?, so an explicit null guard establishes that later member access is safe. A void method can still change an object reached through a reference.
blocks.why: Reusing SelectProject avoids repeating project-ID parsing in view, update, and AI operations. The early return handles failure before the rest of the update logic, reducing nested if blocks.
blocks.before: Main called UpdateStatus(projects) after the user chose 3.
blocks.after: After a successful choice of ID 2, selectedProject refers to the same Inventory object already in projects.
blocks.say: This method takes the project list, asks which project to update, and stops if no project was selected. It does not return a value, but it can change the selected object.
rows: private static void UpdateStatus(List<Project> projects)
A named action that receives our list.
private limits direct access to Program; static means no Program object is required; void means there is no returned result. projects is a parameter, not a fresh collection.
Project? selectedProject = SelectProject(projects);
Get the chosen project or no selection.
SelectProject’s return type permits null. Copying a reference into selectedProject does not clone the object.
if (selectedProject == null) return;
If selection failed or was cancelled, leave this method.
== compares with null. return here returns to Main; it does not itself terminate the application.

blocks.label: Find and return the chosen project
blocks.simple: SelectProject prints the projects, reads the ID you type, and looks for a project whose Id matches it. Typing 2 means "find ID 2", not "take list position 2". The search reaches Inventory and returns a way to reach that existing object.
blocks.technical: ShowProjects is called first and returns after printing. TryParse turns input text into an int without throwing on normal bad input. foreach visits each Project reference. The first equality match returns immediately. If parsing or the search fails, a message is printed and null is returned. Null and "0" are cancellation/end-of-input paths.
blocks.why: A foreach search is explicit and easy to follow for three projects. Indexing with the typed ID would be wrong because list indexes start at zero and IDs need not match positions. A LINQ lookup could be shorter but introduces syntax this demonstration does not need.
blocks.before: input is "2". The three stored Project IDs are 1, 2, 3.
blocks.after: TryParse produces id = 2. ID 1 does not match; ID 2 does. Inventory’s reference is returned to UpdateStatus line 112.
blocks.say: TryParse converts the typed ID safely. The loop compares it with each project’s Id, and returns the matching object. This is why changing selectedProject changes the project the menu later displays.
rows: Project? SelectProject(List<Project> projects)
Find one project; return nothing if selection fails.
Project? is the nullable return type. projects is the list parameter; the returned reference points to an existing object.
ShowProjects(projects);
Display the available IDs before asking.
This call returns void and calculates the listing from current object values.
null check, then zero check
Stop safely for end-of-input or cancellation.
Only call Trim after the null guard. return null signals no selection to the caller.
bool isNumber = int.TryParse(input, out id);
Try converting typed text; remember whether it worked.
TryParse returns bool and assigns the out parameter id. Conversion failure does not throw.
if (isNumber == false)
Reject input such as abc before searching.
This branch returns null after a readable error; successful conversion proceeds to foreach.
foreach (Project project in projects)
Examine each existing project.
The local variable receives each reference in turn.
if (project.Id == id) return project;
Return the matching object.
This returns the same reference; it does not call new or clone the object.

lessons.title: Choose the risk section

blocks.label: Block 1: choose and validate the section
blocks.simple: Read the section as text, check for cancellation, try converting it to a number, then check that the number is 1, 2 or 3. Each decision has its own visible step. For Inventory’s risk, section becomes integer 3.
blocks.technical: TryParse assigns section through an out parameter and returns a bool into isSectionNumber. An early return stops UpdateStatus for invalid input; Main then resumes its loop. The later range check only runs after successful conversion.
blocks.why: Separate conversion and range checks are easier to explain than one combined expression. TryParse safely handles letters and numbers too large for int; the range check handles numbers such as 9.
blocks.before: selectedProject refers to Inventory. You type the string "3".
blocks.after: section is the integer 3. No status has changed yet.
blocks.say: Project selection and section selection are different. ID two chooses Inventory; section three chooses its risk. I validate the number before requesting that section’s allowed statuses.
rows: Task = 1, Milestone = 2, Risk = 3
Ask which part of this project to change.
Section number and project ID are separate inputs.
string? input = Console.ReadLine();
Read the section choice as text.
ReadLine can return null; the next guard handles that before Trim.
bool isSectionNumber = int.TryParse(input, out section);
Try converting the text into a section number.
section receives an int; isSectionNumber receives true or false.
if (isSectionNumber == false)
Stop if conversion failed.
A conversion check is separate from checking the permitted range.
if (section < 1 || section > 3)
Stop if the number is outside 1 through 3.
The || operator means either condition is enough to reject the value.

lessons.title: Show choices, then read Closed

blocks.label: 1 · Call GetAllowedStatuses
blocks.simple: We know the project and section, but still need the legal status choices. This line asks the selected Project for those choices. Because section is 3, the answer will be a two-entry list: Open and Closed.
blocks.technical: GetAllowedStatuses is an instance method declared in Project. selectedProject is the receiver object; section is the argument. The return type List<ItemStatus> means a list of enum values. allowedStatuses is a local variable receiving the returned list reference. The status itself has not been assigned yet.
blocks.why: Keeping the allowed values in Project lets both the menu and ChangeStatus use the same rule. Duplicating one rule in Program and another in Project could let the UI offer a choice that the domain logic rejects.
blocks.before: section = 3; Inventory.RiskStatus = Open.
blocks.after: After this call: allowedStatuses[0] = Open; allowedStatuses[1] = Closed. RiskStatus is still Open.
blocks.say: I call GetAllowedStatuses on the chosen Project. The method returns the allowed enum values, and I store that list in allowedStatuses for the numbered menu.
rows: List<ItemStatus> allowedStatuses
A list of status choices, not a list of projects.
List<T> is reused with a different element type. ItemStatus is an enum; the list is a .NET object.
selectedProject.GetAllowedStatuses(section)
Ask this project which statuses belong to section three.
The dot selects an instance member. Parentheses supply its argument. The method returns a value, so the assignment can capture it.

blocks.label: 2 · Return the allowed statuses
blocks.simple: This method answers the question "which statuses are allowed?" It does not change a status. Section 3 gets Open and Closed. Sections 1 and 2 get the four work statuses. An unsupported section gets an empty list.
blocks.technical: The method takes int section and returns List<ItemStatus>. Each return creates and returns a new list of enum values, then ends this invocation. The first matching branch wins. The final empty list ensures invalid section numbers do not accidentally permit a value.
blocks.why: Enums restrict status spelling at compile time, while this method restricts which enum values make sense for a section. One shared enum is simple but still contains incompatible values; the per-section lists supply that second layer of checking.
blocks.before: The caller passed the number 3 into parameter section.
blocks.after: The first if is true. The returned list is [ItemStatus.Open, ItemStatus.Closed]. The other branches do not run.
blocks.say: GetAllowedStatuses returns choices, not success or failure. For a risk it returns Open and Closed, and returning immediately prevents the work-status branch from running.
rows: public List<ItemStatus> GetAllowedStatuses(int section)
An accessible method that takes a section number and gives back a list.
public allows Program to call it. No static keyword means it is invoked on a Project instance, although this particular rule depends only on the section argument.
if (section == 3)
Check whether we are working with the risk.
== compares values. It does not assign 3 to section.
return new List<ItemStatus> { Open, Closed }
Return exactly the two risk choices in menu order.
The source uses fully qualified ItemStatus values. Their positions in this list, not their underlying enum numbers, determine the menu’s 1 and 2.
section == 1 || section == 2
Task or milestone gets the same work choices.
|| combines two boolean comparisons. Each side must state its comparison explicitly.
return new List<ItemStatus>();
Return no allowed choices for an invalid section.
An empty list is an existing collection with Count zero; it is not null. Contains will be false for any requested value.

blocks.label: 3 · Resume printing and reading
blocks.simple: The loop prints the returned choices as 1. Open and 2. Closed. You type 2. The code checks that this is a valid displayed number. The stored list still uses positions 0 and 1; converting the menu number to a list position happens in the next block.
blocks.technical: The loop separates the zero-based position i, the displayed menuNumber and the enum value status. Later TryParse separately reports conversion success. The range check uses Count before any selected index is read.
blocks.why: The named values make the difference between a menu number, index and enum visible. Safe conversion plus range checking prevents letters or a number outside the list from causing an exception.
blocks.before: allowedStatuses = [Open, Closed]. Count = 2. RiskStatus is still Open.
blocks.after: The menu printed 1 and 2; statusNumber contains integer 2. The object has not changed yet.
blocks.say: The for loop numbers the choices for a person. It adds one only for display. After checking the typed number, the next block subtracts one to read the correct list entry.
rows: for (int i = 0; i < allowedStatuses.Count; i++)
Visit each allowed status in order.
i starts at zero, the test stops before Count, and i++ advances one position.
int menuNumber = i + 1;
Display positions as 1 and 2 for the person.
menuNumber is a display value; i remains the zero-based list index.
ItemStatus status = allowedStatuses[i];
Read the status at this position.
The indexer returns an ItemStatus enum value.
bool isStatusNumber = int.TryParse(input, out statusNumber);
Convert the new input to an integer.
The bool reports conversion success. statusNumber is the separate integer result.
if (isStatusNumber == false)
Reject nonnumeric text.
Returning here prevents any list access or status change.
statusNumber < 1 || statusNumber > allowedStatuses.Count
Accept only the displayed menu range.
This check must happen before indexing the list.

blocks.label: Reference declaration · ItemStatus enum
blocks.simple: An enum is a named set of choices. Instead of spelling a status as loose text every time, the code can use ItemStatus.Open or ItemStatus.Completed. These are values, not methods, classes or calls to AI.
blocks.technical: ItemStatus is an enum type with an integer underlying representation. With these implicit declarations its values run from NotStarted = 0 through Closed = 5. That is separate from the status menu: Closed is menu option 2 for a risk because it is the second entry in that returned list.
blocks.why: An enum avoids string mistakes such as "In progress" versus "InProgress". However, it does not enforce section compatibility by itself, and casts can form undefined values. ChangeStatus checks membership in the allowed list before mutation.
blocks.before: This is a declaration reference. Reading it does not run a menu action.
blocks.after: Methods can accept and return ItemStatus values. GetAllowedStatuses determines the meaningful subset.
blocks.say: ItemStatus defines the names of status values. The risk menu uses only Open and Closed; other values belong to task or milestone choices.
rows: public enum ItemStatus
Declare a type made of named choices.
This is a type declaration, not a method invocation. Enums are value types and are not part of the two authored class count.
Open
One allowed risk-status value.
The fully qualified name is ItemStatus.Open. The dot selects an enum member here, not an object’s method.
Closed
Another risk-status value.
Its implicit underlying number is 5, but the program never asks the user to enter that number. It maps a displayed list position to this value.

lessons.next: Convert menu number 2 into list position 1, then apply Closed.
lessons.goal: We know the project and section, but still need the legal status choices. This line asks the selected Project for those choices. Because section is 3, the answer will be a two-entry list: Open and Closed.

lessons.title: Change the existing Project object

blocks.label: Block 3: choose the value and call the change
blocks.simple: The user entered menu number 2. Subtracting one gives index 1, so the code reads Closed from the list. It then asks the selected Project to apply that value to section 3. The following if runs its body only when the method reports success.
blocks.technical: Three separate variables carry three different meanings: statusIndex is an int position; selectedStatus is an ItemStatus value; statusChanged is the bool returned by the instance method. section and selectedStatus are passed as arguments.
blocks.why: Named intermediate values expose the conversion and the method result. This avoids a method call hidden inside an if condition.
blocks.before: statusNumber = 2; allowedStatuses[1] = Closed; section = 3; Inventory.RiskStatus = Open.
blocks.after: selectedStatus = Closed. Control enters ChangeStatus and will return true if the assignment is valid.
blocks.say: Two minus one selects the second list entry, Closed. I pass that status and section three into ChangeStatus. The if checks its returned success flag before displaying the new health.
rows: int statusIndex = statusNumber - 1;
Turn menu choice 2 into list position 1.
The list is zero-based. This subtraction does not convert the number into an enum.
ItemStatus selectedStatus = allowedStatuses[statusIndex];
Read Closed from position 1.
The list provides the enum value. Closed’s underlying numeric value is unrelated to menu choice 2.
bool statusChanged = selectedProject.ChangeStatus(section, selectedStatus);
Ask the Project to validate and apply the change.
The method acts on the selected instance and returns a bool, which is stored separately from the enum.
if (statusChanged)
Print the new health only after success.
An if accepts a Boolean expression. The named bool makes the meaning of the condition explicit.

blocks.label: Validate, assign, and return success
blocks.simple: This is where the status really changes. First it asks for allowed choices again and checks whether Closed is in them. It is, so the failure return is skipped. Section 3 selects the risk property; that property is assigned Closed, and the method returns true.
blocks.technical: GetAllowedStatuses produces the allowed list. Contains produces the Boolean isAllowed. The guard runs before assignment. Exactly one valid section matches; the method returns true after assigning that section’s property.
blocks.why: Project enforces its own status rules even when a caller bypasses the menu. Separating the list lookup and membership check exposes each step without adding another method.
blocks.before: section = 3, newStatus = Closed, RiskStatus = Open.
blocks.after: RiskStatus is now Closed on Inventory’s existing object. The method returns true; the caller continues inside its if body.
blocks.say: ChangeStatus validates the status even if the caller already checked input. Then it updates the correct property and returns true. The changed object remains in the original list because we are using the same reference.
rows: bool ChangeStatus(int section, ItemStatus newStatus)
Define a method that changes a valid status and reports success.
It is an instance method on one Project, with two parameters and a bool result.
List<ItemStatus> allowedStatuses = GetAllowedStatuses(section);
Get the choices allowed for this section.
The returned list is a local variable in this method, separate from the console method’s list.
bool isAllowed = allowedStatuses.Contains(newStatus);
Check whether the requested status is in that list.
Contains returns a bool and does not modify the list.
if (isAllowed == false) return false;
Reject an incompatible status without changing anything.
An invalid section has an empty allowed list, so this guard also rejects invalid sections.
if (section == 3) RiskStatus = newStatus;
For the risk section, assign the risk status.
Assignment changes this Project object’s private-set property; other objects are unaffected.
return true;
Tell the caller the change succeeded.
This Boolean result is not the new status itself.

blocks.label: Reference declaration · the protected status property
blocks.simple: This property holds the risk status for each individual Project. Other code can read it, but only code inside Project can assign it directly. Closed is its starting value when a new Project is initialized.
blocks.technical: This is an auto-implemented instance property of enum type ItemStatus. lessons.goal: instructions holds what we want the model to do. prompt holds the facts. The temporary request object labels both strings and adds model/settings fields. Serialize turns that object into JSON text for the API.

lessons.title: POST is where the real AI call happens

blocks.label: The actual generation request
blocks.simple: Here is the actual AI request. First StringContent packages our JSON as HTTP content. Next PostAsync sends that content to the local chat address. await waits for the HTTP operation’s result. The result is a response object with status information and content—not yet the plain answer string.
blocks.technical: Evaluation proceeds from the right: client.PostAsync(url, body) returns Task<HttpResponseMessage>; await produces the completed HttpResponseMessage assigned to response. This overload normally buffers response content before completing. EnsureSuccessStatusCode throws for an unsuccessful HTTP status, allowing the catch block to return a message. Both using-declared objects are disposed at the end of the try scope.
blocks.why: The API defines chat generation as a POST with a JSON body. GET model listing cannot generate this reply. We use a .NET method to construct and send the HTTP operation; the application does not execute a curl command or type into Bionic’s chat window. Checking HTTP status catches transport-level failure before parsing a purported answer.
blocks.before: json is request text; client is the sender; destination is http://127.0.0.1:51500/api/v1/chat.
blocks.after: body is StringContent. response is HttpResponseMessage. A successful status allows parsing; failure interrupts the normal path. Project properties remain unchanged.
blocks.say: The real integration line is await client.PostAsync. I pass the local chat URL and JSON body. PostAsync starts the HTTP request, await gives me the completed response object, and I check its status before reading the answer.
rows: using StringContent body = new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");
Wrap the JSON string as the body that HTTP can send.
StringContent is a .NET HttpContent implementation. UTF8 encodes text as bytes; application/json identifies its media type. The variable body holds an object, not a raw string.
client.PostAsync(BionicUrl + "/api/v1/chat", body)
Send a POST request to the chat endpoint with this body.

client is the receiver; PostAsync is its method; the first argument is a URL string and the second is HttpContent. The plus joins two strings. This call crosses the process boundary to Bionic’s local API.
await ... → HttpResponseMessage response
Receive the HTTP result when the operation finishes.
The method call returns Task<HttpResponseMessage>. await unwraps the eventual result; it does not turn the model into a C# object. Main still awaits the whole menu operation.
response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
Stop normal processing if the server reported an unsuccessful status.
An unsuccessful HTTP response causes HttpRequestException. A 2xx success only means the HTTP operation succeeded; it does not prove the generated advice is correct.

lessons.next: Read the response body and extract its final message.
lessons.goal: Here is the actual AI request. First StringContent packages our JSON as HTTP content. Next PostAsync sends that content to the local chat address. await waits for the HTTP operation’s result. The result is a response object with status information and content—not yet the plain answer string.

lessons.title: Unpack the reply and return words

blocks.label: Extract final text and return it
blocks.simple: Read the reply as text, parse that text as JSON, and find the output entries. For each entry, check its type. Keep message words and skip other types. Join the words into one string, check it is not empty, and return it with a label.
blocks.technical: ReadAsStringAsync returns body text into replyText. Parse creates a document; outputs names the output array. The loop reads type first and content only for message entries. += appends each message and a newline to a regular string. Trim removes outside whitespace before returning.
blocks.why: Named intermediate results make reading, parsing and extraction separate steps. A regular string is sufficient for this short reply and removes StringBuilder as an extra concept. Repeated concatenation can copy text, so a large volume of output would justify a different approach.
blocks.before: Illustrative response: output contains a reasoning entry and a message entry with "Risk: Scanner delay. Next action: Use manual numbers."
blocks.after: Only the message text is kept. The returned string begins LOCAL AI ANSWER - qwen/qwen3.5-9b. No assignment writes it to RiskStatus, RiskImpact, or other project properties.
blocks.say: I parse the JSON response, keep only message content, and return a display string. The model cannot change health through this code path because its output is only collected and printed; no property assignment applies it to the project.
rows: string replyText = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
Read the response body into a string.
The awaited result is text. HTTP success has already been checked; text is not yet a parsed document.
using JsonDocument data = JsonDocument.Parse(replyText);
Read the structure of that JSON text.
Parse creates a JsonDocument; the using declaration disposes it at the end of the try scope.
JsonElement outputs = data.RootElement.GetProperty("output");
Locate the output array.
The next loop enumerates JSON entries, not Project objects.
string answer = "";
Start with empty answer text.
answer is a local string variable, separate from the caller’s variable of the same name.
string? type = output.GetProperty("type").GetString();
Read what kind of entry this is.
Only an entry whose type equals message enters the content-reading branch.
string? message = output.GetProperty("content").GetString();
Read this message’s words.
The access stays inside the message branch; non-message entries need no content field.
answer += message + Environment.NewLine;
Join this message to the answer and add a line break.
String concatenation assigns a new string to answer. It never modifies the Project. Environment.NewLine is the platform’s newline sequence.
string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(answer)
Check whether useful answer text was collected.
An HTTP success with no message content still needs a readable failure result.
return ... + answer.Trim();
Return the labelled answer to the caller.
Trim removes outside whitespace. Returning completes the Task<string>; Console.WriteLine in the caller displays it.

blocks.label: The waiting caller resumes and prints it
blocks.simple: The networking helper has finished and we return to the place that was waiting. The returned string is assigned to answer, then WriteLine puts it on screen. This is the final connection between the AI response and the console the audience sees.
blocks.technical: await on Task<string> evaluates to its string result. That result may be a model answer or a friendly error string from a handled failure. After printing, ReviewRiskAsync completes its Task; Main resumes after awaiting it, executes break, and loops to the menu.
blocks.why: Returning text instead of printing deep inside the HTTP code keeps response construction separate from presentation. It also makes failures use the same display path. The app has no separate chat window or live streaming interface.
blocks.before: ExplainRiskAsync is finishing with a labelled answer string.
blocks.after: answer is a string local to ReviewRiskAsync. WriteLine displays it, that method completes, and Main resumes its menu loop.
blocks.say: The response follows a return path: ExplainRiskAsync returns text, ReviewRiskAsync receives and prints it, and Main resumes the menu. This is why the local AI feels like part of the console app.
rows: string answer = await ExplainRiskAsync(client, selectedProject);
This paused statement now receives the completed result.
It does not launch a second request when execution resumes; it completes the original awaited call expression.
Console.WriteLine(answer);
Display exactly the result produced by the helper.
Printing is a console side effect, not a database save or domain update. A later CalculateHealth call still uses the existing Project values.
End of ReviewRiskAsync
Return control to the waiting menu.
The method’s Task completes without a result value. Its caller, Main, can continue after await.

lessons.next: Review the error path, then rehearse the explanation.
lessons.goal: Read the reply as text, parse that text as JSON, and find the output entries. For each entry, check its type. Keep message words and skip other types. Join the words into one string, check it is not empty, and return it with a label.

lessons.title: If AI is unavailable, keep the tracker usable

blocks.label: Expected failure cases
blocks.simple: These are alternative failure paths, not steps that run after every successful reply. If the HTTP or JSON work throws one of these exceptions, the matching catch returns readable text. That text follows the same return-and-print path as a normal result, so the user can continue using the tracker.
blocks.technical: HttpRequestException covers network/request failures and EnsureSuccessStatusCode failures. OperationCanceledException covers the configured timeouts. JsonException handles malformed JSON; KeyNotFoundException and InvalidOperationException cover expected schema access failures. The original exception details are intentionally not exposed in these console messages. Unrelated programming errors are not caught by a blanket catch.
blocks.why: Catching anticipated boundary failures is clearer than letting a disconnected local server terminate the whole demo. Returning a fabricated AI answer would hide the failure, so this helper returns an honest error message. Client cancellation does not guarantee that a separate server stopped generating.
blocks.before: Example: POST receives HTTP 500, or the runtime is unavailable.
blocks.after: EnsureSuccessStatusCode or the HTTP operation throws; catch returns the matching message; WriteLine shows it; the menu returns.
blocks.say: I handle network, timeout and response-format failures at the API boundary. The app reports the problem instead of pretending it received an AI explanation. These catches preserve the console flow, not the correctness of arbitrary generated advice.
rows: catch (HttpRequestException)
Handle a failed HTTP exchange.
A non-success status checked at line 267 follows this path. The message does not distinguish every status or connection cause.
catch (OperationCanceledException)
Handle a request whose wait was cancelled or timed out.
It covers the five-second GET cancellation and the client timeout. It does not establish the execution state of the model in another process.
catch (JsonException)
The body could not be parsed as JSON.
HTTP success and valid JSON are separate checks. A server may return something that is not the expected structured text.
catch (KeyNotFoundException)
The expected JSON field was missing.
For example, GetProperty("output") fails if the response has no output member.
catch (InvalidOperationException)
A JSON value had a kind the code could not use.
For example, calling EnumerateArray on a non-array or GetString on a number follows an unexpected-format path. The exact scope is narrower than catching every Exception.

lessons.goal: These are alternative failure paths, not steps that run after every successful reply. If the HTTP or JSON work throws one of these exceptions, the matching catch returns readable text. That text follows the same return-and-print path as a normal result, so the user can continue using the tracker.

references.title: Project: the properties are the data
references.simple: A class says what each object can hold and do. These declarations give every Project its own identity, one task, one milestone and one risk. Inventory and Training use the same definitions but hold different values. No separate Task, Milestone or Risk class is created in this design.
references.technical: Id and the two ratings are int properties; names, owners, titles, scenario and plan are strings; the dates are DateTime? nullable value types; statuses use ItemStatus. get reads a property and set assigns it. The status setters are private; the others are public. Auto-properties have compiler-generated backing storage. An instance property is different from a local variable inside a method.
references.why: Grouping the data on one Project makes one project easy to pass to health and AI methods. It is intentionally limited to one of each item. Supporting many risks later would call for a collection and usually a separate item type, rather than RiskTitle2, RiskTitle3, and so on.
references.say: Project is the class definition. Each new Project has its own property values. The work and risk fields belong directly to that object, and status changes go through a validation method.

references.title: ShowProjects: a loop, a calculation and counters
references.simple: This method prints a row for every project. Before the loop the three category counters start at zero. Each project supplies a calculated health, then the matching counter increases by one. The summary prints after every project has been visited.
references.technical: foreach iterates existing references in List<Project>. CalculateHealth returns one HealthStatus value. openRisks is either zero or one because the domain has exactly one risk. onTrack++, atRisk++, and offTrack++ increment integers. else if ensures each project contributes to one category. The counters are local values recalculated on every call.
references.why: Computing the list output when requested means status edits are reflected immediately. An array of cached display strings could be shorter to print but would become stale unless explicitly refreshed.
references.say: ShowProjects loops over the list and calculates each object’s current health. Local counters produce the summary, so a later call reflects the values after an update.

references.title: ViewProject: select, get text, print
references.simple: Menu option two selects one project. If selection returns null, it stops. Otherwise it asks the object for a full description and prints the returned text. Nothing is changed by this view operation.
references.technical: SelectProject returns a nullable reference. A null guard exits safely. GetDetails returns a string into details; Console.WriteLine then displays it.
references.why: Reusing SelectProject keeps view/update/AI selection behavior consistent. GetDetails can produce its string separately from the console, so the rule/data class is not responsible for the UI.
references.say: ViewProject selects one existing object, asks for its details string, and displays it. Selection and formatting are separate reusable methods.

references.title: GetDetails: compose the complete project description
references.simple: The returned text combines the project name, manager, health, task, milestone and risk information. CalculateHealth supplies one part; GetRiskDetails supplies the risk part. These methods are being reused, not duplicated.
references.technical: Two local variables store the results of CalculateHealth and GetRiskDetails before interpolation builds the full details string. GetDetails returns text; ViewProject prints it. No property changes occur.
references.why: Keeping one description builder avoids repeating the same labels in every caller. In a larger application the display formatting might move out of the data class; here keeping it near the data is an explicit simplicity tradeoff.
references.say: GetDetails returns the full description. It calls the existing health and risk-detail methods so those rules and labels have one implementation.

references.title: Sample data: why the three starting outcomes differ
references.simple: The method creates three independent Project objects. Website has completed work and a closed risk, so it is OnTrack. Inventory has an open impact-five risk, so it is OffTrack. Training has a closed risk but an overdue unfinished milestone, so it is AtRisk.
references.technical: Object initializers assign public properties after each constructor. Work defaults to NotStarted; risk defaults to Closed. Explicit ChangeStatus calls override selected defaults. DateTime.Today.AddDays creates dates relative to the run date, so the late/future relationships stay consistent. The final list holds these existing references in order.
references.why: Fixed fictional examples demonstrate every health category without a database or interactive data-entry form. They make a reproducible classroom demo. They are not real project telemetry and the risk ratings are not measured by AI.
references.say: I supplied three fictional projects to demonstrate each health rule. The values reset on restart, and dates are relative to today.

references.title: HealthStatus: the result type
references.simple: HealthStatus gives names to the three possible health results. CalculateHealth returns one of them. It is not an object that performs a calculation; the method performs the calculation and chooses a value.
references.technical: HealthStatus is an enum type. Its declaration contains named integral constants, while CalculateHealth returns a value of that type. The Project does not store a separate HealthStatus property, so callers request a fresh result when needed.
references.why: Named values make the health rules easier to read than unexplained numeric codes such as 0, 1 and 2. They also distinguish health categories from the separate ItemStatus enum used for work/risk statuses.
references.say: HealthStatus names the possible results. ItemStatus describes the status of a task, milestone or risk; HealthStatus describes the overall project result.

questions.q: How did you add AI to this C# application?
questions.answer: I connected the console app to a separately running local model through Bionic’s HTTP API. C# builds a message from the selected project, sends it, and prints the returned explanation.
questions.technical: Main creates an HttpClient. ReviewRiskAsync selects and confirms. ExplainRiskAsync validates input, awaits GetLoadedModelAsync, serializes the request, POSTs /api/v1/chat, parses output entries of type message, and returns a string that the caller prints. The model is not embedded in the C# process.
questions.follow: Point to Program.cs line 266, then the replyText/message loop and Console.WriteLine(answer).

questions.q: Which exact command calls the model?
questions.answer: The application does not run a shell command to call Qwen. It calls the C# method client.PostAsync, which sends an HTTP POST to the local chat endpoint.
questions.technical: The exact statement is using HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsync(BionicUrl + "/api/v1/chat", body);. PostAsync is a .NET method, POST is the HTTP operation, and /api/v1/chat is the endpoint path. The body contains serialized JSON.
questions.follow: dotnet run launches the tracker; 4 → 2 → y are console inputs; neither is the literal HTTP request syntax.

questions.q: What did you write, and what did the libraries/runtime provide?
questions.answer: Our application chooses the data, constructs the request, handles the result, and prints it. .NET handles HTTP and JSON. Bionic’s runtime runs the downloaded Qwen model.
questions.technical: Program and Project are the two authored application classes. HttpClient, StringContent, JsonSerializer and JsonDocument are .NET library types. The request uses an anonymous compiler-generated type. Qwen generates text in the separate local runtime; this app does not train a model.
questions.follow: Two authored classes does not mean only two types or objects exist during execution.

questions.q: What must be running before the demo?
questions.answer: The tracker must be running, Bionic’s local API must be listening, and the selected Qwen model must be loaded in memory.
questions.technical: Downloaded means the model file is on disk. Loaded means a runtime instance is resident and appears in loaded_instances. Listening means the HTTP server accepts requests on the configured port. Generating means the runtime is currently producing a reply. These states are related but not identical.
questions.follow: The browser guide at port 8765 is only teaching material; the model API is at port 51500.

questions.q: Why use a local API if the model is on the same computer?
questions.answer: The model is running inside another program. The API gives the tracker a defined way to send it data and receive an answer.
questions.technical: HTTP is a process boundary here, even on loopback. The C# client serializes information; the service interprets its JSON contract and runs inference. Directly calling a method on a Qwen object would require embedding an inference library, which this project does not do.
questions.follow: 127.0.0.1 means this host, not an internet address for the provider.

questions.q: Is ModelKey an API key? Are you using OpenAI credits?
questions.answer: No. ModelKey identifies the local model. This code supplies no secret API key and calls the configured loopback Bionic API.
questions.technical: There is no Authorization header, OpenAI endpoint or cloud fallback in this implementation. The current server setup accepts the local request without a token. Other installations may require authentication; local does not universally mean authentication-free.
questions.follow: A model’s name and a credential serve different purposes. The local machine still supplies memory and compute.

questions.q: Why GET first, then POST?
questions.answer: GET checks whether the exact model is ready. POST sends the request that asks it to generate an explanation.
questions.technical: GET /api/v1/models returns the available-model schema. The code matches key and reads loaded_instances[].id. POST /api/v1/chat receives that selected ID and the prompt. The readiness check does not itself generate text and cannot prevent a state change between the two requests.
questions.follow: If loaded_instances is empty, the helper returns null and the code returns before POST.

questions.q: What exactly is a prompt in this application?
questions.answer: It is a string containing the facts we want Qwen to explain: the fictional project name, C# health, and its risk details.
questions.technical: CalculateHealth and GetRiskDetails provide values, interpolation builds a header, and prompt += riskDetails joins the strings. input receives that prompt. system_prompt receives the separate instructions string. Both are text sent to the runtime.
questions.follow: The wire example shows the full resulting prompt rather than only the code that constructs it.

questions.q: Does input = prompt read something from the keyboard?
questions.answer: No. It puts the existing prompt string into a request property called input.
questions.technical: This assignment is inside an anonymous object initializer. input is the property name required by the API schema; prompt is the local string value. Console.ReadLine is the method that reads keyboard input elsewhere. Identical or similar names do not make these the same thing.
questions.follow: Likewise, model = loadedModelId creates the API field named model using the string stored in our loadedModelId variable.

questions.q: Why convert the request into JSON?
questions.answer: A separate program cannot directly read our in-memory C# object. JSON expresses its named values as text that the API understands.
questions.technical: JsonSerializer.Serialize converts the anonymous request object into a string, preserving the distinction between strings, booleans, numbers and arrays. It escapes embedded quotes and newlines. It does not send the HTTP request or generate the model answer.
questions.follow: Manual string concatenation could create invalid JSON if a scenario contains a quote or newline.

questions.q: Explain every type in the AI call.
questions.answer: client is the sender object. body is the packaged request. response is the returned HTTP response object. The final answer string is extracted afterward.
questions.technical: client has type HttpClient. body is StringContent, usable as HttpContent. PostAsync returns Task<HttpResponseMessage>; await obtains its HttpResponseMessage result. The response body becomes replyText, a string; Parse creates a JsonDocument; the loop collects message content in another string named answer.
questions.follow: An HTTP response includes status and content; it is not already the plain model-answer string.

questions.q: What does await do? Is another thread running the menu?
questions.answer: await lets this method continue after the operation completes. It does not make this menu accept another choice during the AI request.
questions.technical: If an awaited operation is incomplete, the async method can suspend without synchronously blocking a thread just to wait for I/O. But Main awaits ReviewRiskAsync, which awaits ExplainRiskAsync. No concurrent menu-read loop is created. async does not automatically start a background thread or provide a responsive interface.
questions.follow: The Async suffix is a naming convention; async and await have language behavior. The suffix alone does nothing.

questions.q: Why use Task<string>, Task<string?> and Task?
questions.answer: They describe different eventual results: text, possibly missing text, or completion with no result value.
questions.technical: ExplainRiskAsync returns Task<string>; awaiting it yields an answer string. GetLoadedModelAsync returns Task<string?>; awaiting it can yield an ID or null. ReviewRiskAsync and Main return Task because the caller only needs to know when they finish. This .NET Task is unrelated to a project’s task properties.
questions.follow: The question mark applies to the string result in Task<string?>, not to the Task reference itself.

questions.q: Why StringContent, UTF8 and application/json?
questions.answer: They package our text as HTTP content and tell the server how to interpret it.
questions.technical: StringContent is an HttpContent implementation. Encoding.UTF8 chooses how characters become bytes. The media type application/json marks the content as JSON. The raw json variable is a string, while body is an object passed as the second PostAsync argument.
questions.follow: This packaging still happens inside C#; PostAsync is the line that sends it.

questions.q: Why these model settings?
questions.answer: The demo asks for one short final answer without tool integrations or a continuing stored chat.
questions.technical: reasoning is "off", stream and store are false, max_output_tokens is 500, and integrations is empty. The prompt’s 120-word request is separate from the token cap. No temperature is specified, so runtime defaults apply. A model may ignore format instructions; store=false is not a guarantee about every possible log.
questions.follow: Changing stream to true would need different response-reading code; do not claim that a single switch alone adds a streaming console.

questions.q: How does the answer appear in the console?
questions.answer: The helper extracts message text and returns it. The waiting console method receives that string and prints it.
questions.technical: ReadAsStringAsync → replyText string → JsonDocument.Parse → outputs array → type check → message string → answer string → return. ReviewRiskAsync receives that returned text and calls Console.WriteLine(answer). Main then resumes the menu.
questions.follow: Returning a value and printing it are different operations.

questions.q: What if output contains more than one entry?
questions.answer: It checks every entry and joins the message text into one answer. Non-message entries are skipped.
questions.technical: The loop checks each entry’s type and reads content only for message entries. Each message is concatenated to the answer string with Environment.NewLine. Other output types are ignored. For this short reply, a regular string keeps the code simple; very large repeated concatenation would copy more text.
questions.follow: The illustrative response in the wire panel contains an ignored entry so you can predict the output.

questions.q: What if the API returns HTTP 500?
questions.answer: The response-status check stops the normal path and a catch returns a readable failure message.
questions.technical: EnsureSuccessStatusCode at line 267 throws HttpRequestException for an unsuccessful HTTP status. The catch at line 289 handles it, so the message-content loop is not reached. The caller prints that error string and the menu returns.
questions.follow: A 200 response can still contain invalid JSON or inaccurate advice; HTTP success is only one level of success.

questions.q: If the request times out, did Qwen stop generating?
questions.answer: We can only say the tracker stopped waiting for that request. We cannot conclude that the separate model process stopped.
questions.technical: Cancellation and timeout affect the client’s awaited operation. They are caught as OperationCanceledException. Server cancellation behavior is separate and the application does not query it. Readiness has a five-second token; chat uses the client’s 120-second timeout.
questions.follow: Do not describe the timeout as killing Bionic or unloading the model.

questions.q: What exactly does AI decide in this project?
questions.answer: It decides the wording of a risk explanation and suggested action. C# supplies the ratings, score, status and health.
questions.technical: The returned model text is never parsed into assignments to Project properties. CalculateRiskScore and CalculateHealth run independently of the response. Prompt instructions also ask the model to preserve the supplied data, but the stronger reason it cannot update the object through this path is the absence of assignments from its output.
questions.follow: If it writes "OnTrack" for Inventory, the next C# calculation is still OffTrack while the open high-impact risk remains.

questions.q: Is 20/25 an 80% chance the project fails?
questions.answer: No. It is the product of two classroom ratings and is used as a priority score.
questions.technical: The score is not fitted to observed failure rates or calibrated against outcomes. The health rule directly checks Open status and impact >=4; it does not threshold the product. This is a demonstration of software logic and AI explanation, not a validated forecasting system.
questions.follow: Likelihood 1 and impact 5 still produce OffTrack when the risk is Open.

questions.q: Why not let the model calculate health too?
questions.answer: Visible C# rules make the same facts produce the same category. AI adds a written explanation without controlling that category.
questions.technical: Free-form model outputs vary and would need parsing, validation and a defined scoring policy before updating state. This implementation avoids that extra complexity. A useful future design could compare suggestions with a rule result, but that behavior is not implemented here.
questions.follow: Do not claim the model quantitatively estimates the supplied ratings; those are in CreateSampleProjects.

questions.q: Does the model see all my files or the whole project?
questions.answer: This request sends the selected fictional project name, calculated health and formatted risk details.
questions.technical: There is no filesystem tool, repository upload, document search or code attachment in this request. integrations is empty. A model only receives what this request provides plus its existing trained capabilities; the application does not let it inspect the live Project object or automatically edit source files.
questions.follow: This describes this code path, not every feature the separate Bionic application might have.

questions.q: Is this training, fine-tuning or inference?
questions.answer: It is inference: using an already-trained model to produce a response to a new input.
questions.technical: The application sends a chat request and reads a reply. It does not update model weights, provide a training loop or launch a fine-tuning job. Adding a system prompt changes the context for this request, not the model’s learned parameters.
questions.follow: The 9B model name is not a count of our application classes or a measure of risk accuracy.

questions.q: Why can you change a project through selectedProject?
questions.answer: selectedProject points to the same object stored in the list. Selection does not make a copy of that object.
questions.technical: The Project class is a reference type. SelectProject returns a copied reference value, and the receiving variable can reach the same object. Mutating its RiskStatus through ChangeStatus is visible on later list reads. Reassigning the local selectedProject variable to a different object would be a different operation.
questions.follow: The list, each Project, and each variable referring to them are separate concepts.

questions.q: Where are inheritance and encapsulation used?
questions.answer: The two application classes do not inherit from each other. Status values are protected by private setters and changed through a checking method.
questions.technical: This design uses objects, instance methods and encapsulation, not a custom inheritance hierarchy. Like other C# classes they implicitly derive from object. Public rating properties remain freely assignable; only the AI boundary checks their range, so do not claim every property is validated.
questions.follow: One class calling another class’s method is not inheritance.

questions.q: Why two classes instead of putting everything in Main?
questions.answer: Project keeps one project’s data and rules together. Program handles user input, output and the API connection.
questions.technical: This separates domain operations from interaction. It also limits the data model to one task, milestone and risk per project. One giant Main method could use fewer method declarations but would interleave validation, calculations, sample data, HTTP and display code.
questions.follow: There is no claim that two classes is the best design for a larger application.

questions.q: How do you know the integration works?
questions.answer: The readability refactor builds cleanly and passes 106 checks using simulated API replies. An earlier version also received a real Qwen reply through this console integration.
questions.technical: The current checks cover status and health behavior, invalid selections, cancellation, request fields, exact loaded-model selection, multiple message entries, ignored non-message entries, empty/malformed replies and error paths. A new live model call was not made for this refactor; the recorded reply is explicitly a previous test.
questions.follow: You should distinguish simulated checks from a real model call and a saved reply from the current live reply.

commands.what: Build and start the console application without attaching the debugger.
commands.expect: The tracker heading and options 1–5 appear in a console window.
commands.generation: No model request until you select AI and confirm.
commands.why: This is a keyboard shortcut, not C# syntax or an HTTP verb.

commands.where: Inside the running tracker; press Enter after each entry
commands.what: Choose Explain a risk, choose Inventory by project ID, then confirm.
commands.expect: The tracker checks the loaded model and, if ready, sends a real AI request and prints its reply.
commands.generation: Yes, if the risk is open and the model is ready.
commands.why: Use a fresh app session or reopen the risk with 3 → 2 → 3 → 1 first. Do not paste these numbers into PowerShell.

commands.what: Send an HTTP POST containing the prepared JSON body.
commands.expect: Awaiting PostAsync returns an HttpResponseMessage, even when the server reports HTTP 500. Connection failures or cancellation can throw. The following EnsureSuccessStatusCode call rejects unsuccessful HTTP status codes.
commands.generation: Yes, this is the actual generation request.
commands.why: You point to this code during a presentation. Do not type it into the tracker’s menu or a shell.

commands.where: Between the C# process and the local API server
commands.what: Identify the network operation performed by PostAsync.
commands.expect: The API responds with JSON, including an output array on a successful normal reply.
