study.title: Start here: two classes and one starting point
study.read: A class defines what an object can hold and do. Project defines one project’s information and rules. Program controls the sequence. Execution starts inside Main, which creates sample projects and one HTTP client before showing the menu.
study.technical: List<Project> is a list type; projects is a variable holding a reference to that list. CreateSampleProjects() is a method call returning it. static means Main runs without a Program object; async supports await, and Task represents asynchronous completion. new HttpClient creates the sender without sending a request.
study.why: Two classes keep the project rules together and the console/AI actions together. The source files are containers for code; .cs does not mean every file is a class.
study.say: “Main starts the application. It creates the example projects and prepares one client that later sends the AI requests.”

blocks.label: Start in Main; comments explain the setup

study.title: Follow creation: one Project object has its own values
study.read: CreateSampleProjects uses new Project to create Website, Inventory and Training. The constructor copies the ID, name and manager into each object. The initializer supplies its other properties. The method returns a list containing these three objects.
study.technical: A constructor runs when new creates the object. Properties such as RiskImpact belong to that instance. ItemStatus and HealthStatus are enums: fixed named choices. They are not extra classes. Neither authored class inherits from the other.
study.why: Fictional sample data gives a repeatable demo without a database. Objects live in memory, so changes reset after restarting. The other two examples follow Inventory’s pattern.
study.say: “Project is the definition. Inventory System is one object created from it, with its own manager, statuses and risk ratings.”

blocks.label: new Project calls the constructor before the initializer
The constructor copies the incoming values
After the constructor returns, assign the remaining properties

study.title: Menu 1: list projects and count their health
study.read: Main repeats a menu. Choosing 1 calls ShowProjects. Its foreach loop visits every project, asks it for health, prints one row and adds one to the appropriate counter. After the loop it prints the totals.
study.technical: foreach reads each object reference from the list. CalculateHealth returns a HealthStatus enum. ++ adds one to an integer. ShowProjects returns void, meaning it supplies no result value. Main continues after the call.
study.why: A loop performs the same steps for all three objects. Fresh calculations reflect a status you changed earlier; a stored health label could become outdated.
study.say: “This method lists the projects and counts the health categories. Each Project calculates its own health; the console method displays it.”

blocks.label: One loop displays rows and builds the summary

study.title: Menu 2: select the existing object, get text, print it
study.read: ViewProject calls SelectProject, which displays the IDs and reads your choice. It converts the text safely and searches for a matching ID. ViewProject receives that existing object, gets its details text and prints the text.
study.technical: Project? allows a project reference or null. Zero, end-of-input or an invalid choice returns null. The null guard stops ViewProject before it uses a missing object. GetDetails calls CalculateHealth and GetRiskDetails, then returns a formatted string.
study.why: Selection is shared by viewing, updating and AI. Returning the existing reference lets later updates affect the same object in the list. Formatting text and printing it are separate actions.
study.say: “SelectProject finds the object. GetDetails prepares its description. Console.WriteLine puts that description on screen.”

blocks.label: The three visible actions: select, format, print
Project prepares the description

study.title: Menu 3: turn typed text into a safe menu choice
study.read: For Inventory’s risk, choose 3 → 2 → 3 → 2. The last 2 is text from the keyboard. TryParse attempts to turn it into integer 2. A separate check rejects numbers outside the displayed menu.
study.technical: TryParse returns a bool into isStatusNumber and assigns the integer through out statusNumber. The bool answers “did conversion work?”; the integer answers “which number?”. return stops this update early when a check fails.
study.why: Separating conversion from range checking makes each decision readable. Letters and a number such as 99 fail for different reasons. No object changes until all selections have passed.
study.say: “I first check that the input is a number. Then I check that it names one of the choices. This keeps invalid input from changing a status.”

blocks.label: Conversion and range checking are separate steps

study.title: Apply the change, then calculate the new health
study.read: GetAllowedStatuses returns [Open, Closed] for section 3. Menu number 2 becomes list index 1, giving Closed. ChangeStatus checks the allowed list and assigns RiskStatus. Inventory’s future milestone and closed risk then produce OnTrack.
study.technical: The menu number, list index, enum value and bool success result are different values. private set restricts direct status assignment to Project. Health checks an open high-impact risk first, then other open risks, then a late unfinished milestone.
study.why: Project validates its own rules even if another caller skips the console checks. Named Booleans make the health decision readable. HasValue protects a missing date; due today is not late.
study.say: “The selected enum changes one property on the existing object. CalculateHealth then reads the updated facts and returns the current health category.”

blocks.label: Menu number → index → enum → method result
The object validates and assigns
Read the named facts and apply the health rules

study.title: Menu 4: preview the facts and confirm AI
study.read: Reopen Inventory with 3 → 2 → 3 → 1; then choose 4 → 2 → y. ReviewRiskAsync previews the open risk and confirms AI. GetRiskDetails builds the description. CalculateRiskScore gives 4 × 5 = 20, a ranking rather than a failure probability.
study.technical: This score is a ranking, not an 80% failure probability, and health uses separate rules. Confirmation text is trimmed and lowercased. On y, ExplainRiskAsync receives the selected Project and the shared HttpClient.
study.why: The preview lets you see what is sent. Reusing GetRiskDetails keeps the displayed facts and prompt consistent. C# keeps authority over ratings and health; AI supplies an explanation.
study.say: “The score is ordinary multiplication in C#. I show the risk facts, confirm the request, and pass those facts to the AI method.”

blocks.label: C# calculates the priority score
The same risk text supports display and AI

study.title: AI readiness: locate the loaded Qwen instance
study.read: Bionic runs separately from the tracker. The API listens at 127.0.0.1:51500. GetLoadedModelAsync sends GET /api/v1/models, finds qwen/qwen3.5-9b and returns a loaded instance ID. No matching loaded instance means no chat request.
study.technical: ModelKey identifies the model; it is not a password. loadedModelId is the returned instance identifier. Task<string?> means this async method eventually supplies text or null. The five-second cancellation token limits the readiness wait.
study.why: The app checks the exact intended model instead of choosing whichever model appears first. A model downloaded on disk is not necessarily loaded in memory. GET asks about readiness; POST requests generation.
study.say: “The tracker talks to a local API. First it checks that Qwen is loaded and obtains the identifier needed for the chat request.”

blocks.label: The caller receives a loaded ID or returns a setup message
Look through model entries and loaded instances

study.title: Build the AI request: facts, instructions and JSON
study.read: ExplainRiskAsync stores the health and risk description in named variables. prompt joins those facts into text. instructions asks for Risk, Why and Next action. A temporary request object labels those strings and the settings; Serialize turns it into JSON.
study.technical: In model = loadedModelId, model is the API field name and loadedModelId is our variable. input receives prompt; system_prompt receives instructions. JSON is structured text that the other program understands. It is not the live Project object.
study.why: Separate strings expose what information is sent and what answer is requested. Serialization handles quotes and escaping. The API request uses an anonymous object, so no extra authored request class is needed.
study.say: “I package the facts and instructions in the format Bionic expects. The local model receives text about this risk, not access to my whole program.”

blocks.label: First build the prompt from named results
Then serialize the request fields

study.title: Send the request, then unpack the reply
study.read: StringContent packages the JSON as an HTTP body. PostAsync sends it to /api/v1/chat. await receives the response. After checking HTTP success, the code reads replyText, parses its JSON and collects only message content into answer.
study.technical: PostAsync returns Task<HttpResponseMessage>; await supplies the response object. Parse reads the JSON structure. A foreach loop checks type before reading content. += joins each message to an ordinary string. Trim removes outside whitespace.
study.why: This is the actual generation request. GET, new HttpClient and WriteLine do not generate answers. A regular string is enough for this short reply. Selecting message entries keeps unrelated output out of the displayed answer.
study.say: “PostAsync sends the real request. I parse the reply and keep the message text. The AI method returns that string, and ReviewRiskAsync prints it.”

blocks.label: The exact local AI call
Read → parse → select messages → return text

study.title: Finish the path: failures, the menu, and exit
study.read: If networking or JSON reading fails, an appropriate catch returns a readable message. It is printed through the same path as an answer. After the menu action finishes, Main shows the menu again. Choosing 5 exits.
study.technical: return in ExplainRiskAsync supplies a string to its caller. return in Main ends the program. break exits the switch, allowing while to repeat. The console waits while its AI call is pending. No assignment applies generated text to Project properties.
study.why: Expected API failures should not terminate the whole tracker. There is no fake live-answer fallback. A timeout ends the client’s wait but does not prove the separate model stopped generating.
study.say: “A request can return advice or an error message. Either way the user gets the menu back. Option five returns from Main and ends the program.”

blocks.label: Returned text reaches the same console
One example of a handled failure
Exit returns from Main

study.title: Check your understanding, then rehearse for eight minutes
study.read: Try three predictions before revealing the answers. Explain the sequence in your own words rather than memorizing punctuation. Then open Rehearse for the timed script and demo. This short path covers each method’s role; the detailed tabs explain individual expressions.
study.technical: Comments beginning with // explain intent to readers and do not run. The displayed code is copied from the application, including its comments and current file/line locations. Select a code block when a step contains more than one.
study.why: An eight-minute talk can cover the complete design, the important statements, every method’s role and a demo. Reading every source line aloud would take longer. The detailed reference remains available for follow-up questions.
study.say: “I can follow one input from the menu to the changed object, and one risk from its facts to the local model and back to the console.”

predictions.q: Inventory’s open risk has impact 5. You close it; its milestone is in the future. What health is returned?
predictions.a: OnTrack. The open-risk branch no longer applies, and the milestone is not late. The ratings still exist, but a closed risk no longer triggers the risk-health rule.

predictions.q: The model file is downloaded, but loaded_instances is empty. Does the tracker send POST?
predictions.a: No. The readiness method returns null, and ExplainRiskAsync returns a setup message before reaching PostAsync.

predictions.q: Qwen writes “this project is safe” even though C# says OffTrack. Which project value changes?
predictions.a: None. The reply is collected into a string and printed. There is no assignment from model output to health, ratings or status; C# still returns OffTrack.
